Gaza: Two Drones an Hour, Three “Martyrs” in One Family

At noon, an Israeli drone struck a tent near the Kuwaiti Hospital in al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis. Less than an hour later, another drone hit a home in northern Nuseirat.

Palestinian reporters described injuries in both places. The first strike hit the tent of the al-Rai family in a displacement camp. The second hit the home of Raafat Abu Khabiza. 

In the official IDF version, the same hour contained two threats removed from the map: one Palestinian Islamic Jihad operative in Khan Younis and one Hamas operative in Nuseirat, both allegedly advancing attack plans. 

The agreement, then, is functioning normally. It includes targeted killings.

By evening, the first target was identified as Tareq Anwar al-Rai, described by Israeli sources as a Palestinian Islamic Jihad operative. Palestinian accounts called him the third “martyr” from his family.

That word has a family archive behind it.

His brother, Mohammed al-Rai, was killed in an Israeli airstrike in Rafah in 2007. Israeli security sources identified him as the militant who fired the grenade from a mobile launcher during the 2004 APC disaster on the Philadelphi Route, which killed five Israeli soldiers transporting explosives.

Another brother, Khamis al-Rai, was described as a senior Islamic Jihad commander and was killed in Rafah in 2015.

Three brothers. Three Israeli strikes. More than two decades of attrition, promotion, revenge and obituary language.

Israel calls it removing immediate threats. Gaza calls it martyrdom. Both descriptions avoid the more durable fact: a militant organization and the military targeting it have spent a generation turning a family name into a recurring file.

Ali al-Taher’s White Night

One explosive drone, three seriously wounded Israeli soldiers, and a whole night of war machinery started moving.

Israel’s security establishment believes Hezbollah launched Saturday’s drone from the underground complex beneath the Ali al-Taher ridge near Nabatieh. 

The Israeli reading is blunt: the fighters inside are not preparing to surrender. They are preparing to fight. The IDF describes the site as Hezbollah’s regional “nerve center,” with dozens of operatives believed to be underground. 

Then came the long night.

Israeli aircraft struck the ridge and areas around Kfar Rumman, Deir Siryan and Qantara. Heavy artillery hit Nabatieh al-Fawqa. Lebanese media reported illumination rounds over the ridge, fires on its slopes and extensive Israeli aircraft activity. Hezbollah-linked outlets said the group fired anti-aircraft missiles toward the planes. 

By Monday morning, strikes and shelling had also reached al-Mansouri, Kafra and Majdal Zoun. Reports said two civilians were wounded in a drone strike in Kafra. 

The ridge has become a tunnel with a town attached.
Israeli and Lebanese reports describe a widening ground operation involving infantry, air power and other forces. Israeli officials say they want to destroy the underground system and remove Hezbollah from the area. 

Lebanese sources describe exchanges of fire and a campaign to take control of the hill. The contest is no longer about one drone. It is about who owns the ground above a buried command structure. 

Iran’s reported threat to fire missiles at Israel if Hezbollah and IRGC intelligence material is captured completes the picture. 

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said “no account on any front will remain unsettled” and promised forceful action to protect Israeli soldiers and civilians. The language is designed to make an operation around a single ridge sound like a regional ledger. 

A Lebanese political source told Nidaa al-Watan that Hezbollah is escalating militarily in order to derail the possibility of direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations, while waiting for an Iranian green light for a broader confrontation.
